transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-16 15:00 PDT
Duration: 50 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Sam (Redwood CSM), Carlos (Waveform CTO), Aisha (Waveform SRE), Ben (Waveform ML Eng), Marta (Waveform Product)

Summary:
Short weekly sync to review last 48h pilot telemetry, discuss persistent tail-latency spikes around burst windows, agree on tuning steps for continuous batching and concurrency targets, and set the next ramp test. Customer emphasized need for stable 95th percentile latency under 450ms for synchronous API paths; they will provide fuller request distribution.

Topics:
- Recent pilot results (throughput, p95/p99, kv-cache misses)
- Continuous-batching param tuning (max batch wait, targeting, pad-trimming)
- Concurrency targets and per-GPU inflight limits
- Queue shaping/backpressure and burst smoothing
- Next ramp test and artifacts to share

Action items (read out at end of call): Jordan to share telemetry sheet; Aisha to upload traces; Priya to run sim; schedule kernel deep-dive if needed.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick check, audio ok?
[00:03] Carlos (CTO): Yep, loud and clear.
[00:06] Jordan (AE): Cool. This is our weekly check for Waveform pilot throughput. Priya and I will go through the results from the last 48 hours and then pivot into tuning items. Aisha, Ben — do you want to call out anything up front?
[00:18] Aisha (SRE): Uh briefly — we've seen bursts where p95 jumps from like 220ms to 700ms for a 90 second window. It correlates with midday traffic and some longer prompts, but there's also KV cache evictions. We're concerned about the tails for synchronous requests.
[00:35] Ben (ML Eng): Yeah the payload distribution changed a bit when we rolled the named-entity routing on Tuesday; more multi-turn context came through.
[00:44] Priya (SE): Got it. Thanks. I pulled the telemetry and did a quick breakdown — I'm sharing my screen, hope that's okay.
[00:50] Marta (Product): Fine.
[00:52] [01:00] Priya (SE): Okay first slide, rolling 5m throughput — average steady at ~420 rps, burst peaks to 1.8k rps for ~60-120s. Concurrent requests at the peaks push per-GPU inflight to ~22. That is where we start seeing queue saturation and batch head-of-line waits extend, so p95 balloons.
[01:25] Jordan (AE): Quick clarifier — when you say 'concurrent requests' that's at the Redwood routing layer or customer side?
[01:31] Priya (SE): That's at our edge routing -> the number of active requests routed to the same GPU pool. It's after our smart routing but before batching aggregation.
[01:40] Carlos (CTO): We're running with the default continuous-batching config, right? No custom max batch setting yet?
[01:45] Priya (SE): Correct, default continuous-batching parameters. We did set max_concurrency_hint to 6 in one lane but most traffic currently goes through the default lane.
[01:56] [02:00] Ben (ML Eng): We're also seeing some KV cache churn — I think key cardinality spiked because of extra user metadata in the context, so misses go up which increases decode time.
[02:10] Priya (SE): That matches the cache-miss counters — miss rate increased to ~18% during peaks vs 3% baseline. When the KV cache misses, the model has to recompute some prefixes causing extra latency per token, which compounds.
[02:24] Aisha (SRE): Is there a way to pin heavier traffic onto a dedicated lane to prevent noisy neighbor effects?
[02:31] Jordan (AE): Yes, we can create a dedicated route/rule to pin a percentage of traffic to a lane with stricter concurrency caps. That's essentially a soft reserved lane — we can do that for the midday window.
[02:41] [03:00] Priya (SE): Proposed tuning bundle: 1) Set max_batch_wait from 30ms to 18ms for the default lane to reduce head-of-line waits; 2) Lower max_inflight per-worker from 24 -> 16 to cap per-GPU concurrency; 3) Enable prefix trimming for known long metadata fields so they don't blow KV keys; 4) Create a dedicated 'burst' lane with burst_capacity=2x for controlled overflow instead of saturating the default pool.
[03:28] Carlos (CTO): What's the impact on throughput if we lower inflight? Will we lose peak RPS?
[03:34] Priya (SE): Short answer: potentially a small reduction in max instantaneous RPS, but we expect much tighter tails and better steady-state throughput because batching will be more efficient. The platform tends to trade a tiny bit of peak for far lower p95/p99. We can also use burst_capacity and temporary autoscale to recover peak without hurting the default lane.
[03:54] Ben (ML Eng): Are you saying we should accept lower instantaneous throughput to get latency SLO? We need to quantify that — like, are we talking 3-6% drop or 15%?
[04:04] Priya (SE): From similar pilots I'd estimate 5-8% at most. But we should run the controlled 2-hour ramp to measure exactly.
[04:12] [04:30] Jordan (AE): Also food for thought: quantization profile — we haven't switched to int8 for your model yet. That will help token throughput but we need to verify output quality. That could be a separate canary.
[04:23] Carlos (CTO): We want to keep quality stable for classification tasks; quantization may change scores. Let's treat quant as separate. For this sync let's focus on batching/concurrency.
[04:37] Marta (Product): Our primary target is p95 < 450ms for sync inference. Anything that risks classification regression is risky.
[04:44] [05:00] Priya (SE): Understood. Ok let's walk through the telemetry details — I'm calling out three windows: baseline (off-peak), ramp up, and burst plateau. During ramp we see batch sizes collapse due to many small requests and some singletons which kills efficiency. Continuous-batching parameters can help by holding small requests a tiny bit longer to fill batches without adding too much latency.
[05:27] Ben (ML Eng): How do you set the wait tunable so small requests don't get held forever?
[05:31] Priya (SE): It's max_batch_wait and also a per-route min_batch_size trigger. The idea is to reduce wait to something like 12-20ms for default lane; that buys batching for many small requests. If you have strict SLO per request <200ms, you'd pick a smaller wait.
[05:46] [06:00] Aisha (SRE): Would prefix trimming affect any inference correctness — we add user_id and session_id in the prompt, we can't drop those.
[06:08] Priya (SE): We won't drop functional tokens. Prefix trimming targets nonessential metadata fields, typically appended user agent strings or long trace debug dumps. We can also canonicalize session keys to a shorter stable digest for the KV key. That's safe.
[06:22] Carlos (CTO): That digest approach sounds promising. Ben, can you add a stage to hash arbitrary metadata keys before the request hits Redwood?
[06:30] Ben (ML Eng): Yep, we can do that quickly, maybe today's release.
[06:33] [07:00] Priya (SE): Great. Next, queue shaping/backpressure — when inflight > threshold we can return 429s or queue at the edge with an adaptive delay. For sync flows you prefer queueing with a short eta rather than immediate 429, right?
[07:15] Marta (Product): We want the user to see a small spinner, not an error, as long as it's under 1s. So a short queue is fine but must preserve SLO.
[07:23] Jordan (AE): Actionable plan: we'll configure adaptive queueing target max extra wait <300ms and fallback to 429 if queue time > 900ms. That is configurable per-route.
[07:37] [08:00] Priya (SE): I'm going to propose a baseline config to test in the ramp:
- default lane: max_batch_wait 18ms, min_batch_size 2, max_inflight_per_worker 16
- burst lane: dedicated rule for 20% of traffic during 11:30-13:30 PT, burst_capacity: 2, autoscale aggressiveness +1
- KV: server-side metadata canonicalization + trim rules for long fields

(brief chuckle)
[08:29] Ben (ML Eng): If we do per-route queueing, do you have metrics to show user-perceived latency? We need instrumentation to show time-in-queue vs model-decode time.
[08:39] Priya (SE): Yes we will add telemetry columns: queue_time_ms, batch_wait_ms, model_decode_ms, kv_miss_ms. I'll push an updated dashboard.
[08:48] [09:00] Carlos (CTO): One more ask — can Redwood give a kernel-level flame or sample profile when p95 spikes? We want to know if it's CPU-side scheduling or GPU decode stalls.
[09:10] Priya (SE): We can run a lightweight profiler during the next controlled ramp. It requires brief elevated permissions to capture perf counters. Priya (laughs) — or I can hand that to our infra team.
[09:20] Jordan (AE): We'll coordinate offline on the permissions.
[09:24] [10:00] Aisha (SRE): For the ramp test itself, what traffic generator do you recommend? We currently use k6 for load but need something that replays real request distributions including multi-turn context.
[10:33] Priya (SE): Best is our pilot harness (we provided it) with your recorded request histogram; if not available, use Gatling or k6 with a custom arrival curve. Key is to preserve payload lengths and inter-arrival CV.
[10:45] Ben (ML Eng): We'll try the Redwood harness. Can you re-issue the recording script?
[10:50] Jordan (AE): Yes — I'll drop updated instructions and the harness link in the deck after the call.
[10:55] [11:00] Priya (SE): Ok so immediate A/B config we'll push tonight to the staging lane: the default lane tunables I mentioned. We'll monitor telemetry and if initial improvements are seen we'll roll to pilot fleet for the 7/18 ramp test.
[11:12] Marta (Product): If this reduces p95 to <450ms we're probably ready to expand the pilot. What's your confidence level?
[11:18] Priya (SE): I'm cautiously optimistic. We've seen similar patterns improved in other pilots by 30-60% on p95 with the combo of trimming, tighter batch-waits, and per-worker inflight caps.
[11:28] [12:00] Carlos (CTO): What about billing — if we move traffic to a burst lane with autoscale, does that change cost profile? Need a rough estimate for finance.
[12:38] Jordan (AE): It'll add some peak cost but it's transient. We can model the cost delta post-ramp — probably 6-14% uplift during burst windows depending on autoscale aggressiveness.
[12:50] Ben (ML Eng): Any risk with model fallback? We considered having a smaller distilled model for heavy bursts.
[12:58] Priya (SE): Fallback is an option; Redwood supports automated fallback policy by architecture compatibility. But fallback implies quality change and clients must opt in. It's worth keeping as a safety valve.
[13:08] [13:30] Aisha (SRE): Ok let's recap the concrete steps so nothing gets lost.
Jordan (AE): Jordan: send pilot telemetry spreadsheet and the harness link; Priya: push staging config and produce batch-size histogram sim; Aisha: upload 24h tail traces; Ben: implement hashing of metadata keys for KV canonicalization; Marta/Carlos: confirm p95 target and any tolerance windows.
[13:45] Priya (SE): I'll also add per-route queue_time telemetry and the KV miss drill-down to the dashboard.
[13:52] Jordan (AE): We'll set the 2-hour ramp for Saturday 7/18 08:00 PT, unless you prefer a different window.
[13:59] Carlos (CTO): That works.
[14:05] Jordan (AE): Perfect. Any final Qs?
[14:08] Marta (Product): No, just please keep us posted on the initial staging results.
[14:12] Aisha (SRE): One last thing — SOC2 audit team asked about audit logs for route changes. Can you attach the change diff when you push the config?
[14:20] Jordan (AE): Yes we'll include the config diff and the change ticket in the shared thread.
[14:26] [15:00] Jordan (AE): Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes.
[15:02] Carlos (CTO): Thanks all.

End of transcript.
